Thus, Thomas concludes, no similitude can lead our intellect to God.105 Once again we notice that Thomas’s discussion is rather far from Pico’s understanding of this issue. Thesis 23 takes us directly to the conceptual tension between ‘one’ (unum) and ‘being’ (ens), which Pico was going to address in his De ente et uno (1490– 1491), a work which stands at the centre of Chapter 16 together with its critical reception by Antonio Cittadini. Interestingly, we find in William Ockham a link between theses 23 and 24: William suggests an analogy between the relation ens and unum on the one hand, and passio and subiectum on the other. According to William, ‘being’ and ‘one’ refer to the same thing, just as, generally speaking, ‘quality’ (passio) and ‘subject’ (subiectum). For this

For this reason the predication of one to the other is necessary.119 One can only won- der whether Pico had this analogy of William at the back of his mind while working of theses 23 and 24. This might also be a reminder that Pico uses many different sources, some in a direct and a straightforward fashion and some in an indirect fashion.
